Goiter

claims.claim_text: Specific foods that disrupt the thyroid ('goitrogens'). Wallach names the foods and additives that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism and produce thyroid disease. Two groups stand out: (1) nitrates and nitrites — the preservatives in processed and cured meats: ham, bacon, sausage, bologna, salami, pastrami, pepperoni, jerky and deli meats; and (2) cruciferous vegetables — broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and cauliflower.
claims.verbatim:
Many foods and food additives are known

“goitrogens” because they interfere with the normal thyroid

metabolism and produce thyroid disease. These substances

include nitrates and nitrites (i.e. ham, bacon, sausage, bologna,
salami, pastrami, pepperoni, jerky, deli-meats, etc.) and
cruciferous vegetables (i.e. broccoli, Brussel sprouts, cabbage,
cauliflower, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Indium — a rare, soft, bluish-white metal. Wallach notes it resists corrosion, leaves a residue when rubbed on other metals, and emits a strange 'shrieking' noise when bent; commercially it is a byproduct of refining zinc. It was discovered in 1863 by the German chemist Ferdinand Reich while studying zinc ore, identified by the bright violet light it gives off under spectroscopic analysis (splitting its light into a color fingerprint), and named from the Latin 'indicum' meaning 'violet' or 'indigo.'
claims.verbatim:
In-Indium is found in igneous rocks at 0.05 to 1.0 ppm,

terrestrial plants at 0.62 ppm, and terrestrial animals at 0.016

ppm. Indium is a rare, soft, bluish-white metal that is corrosion
resistant. When it is vigorously rubbed against other metals it
will leave small residues of itself; when bent rapidly, indium
emits a bizarre “shrieking” noise. Commercial sources of
indium are produced as a byproduct of refining zinc.

Indium was discovered in 1863 by the German chemist
Ferdinand Reich while studying zinc ore. It was identified by
the bright violet light that it gave off during spectroscopic
analysis. Its name is taken from the Latin word indicum, which
translates to “violet” or “indigo.”

claims.claim_text: Iridium — one of the hardest and most corrosion-resistant metals known, a precious metal similar to platinum. It was discovered in 1803 by the English chemist Smithson Tennant, using the same process that led him to osmium: he isolated it from the residues left when platinum ores are treated with aqua regia (a nitric + hydrochloric acid mixture that dissolves gold and platinum). Tennant named it after the Latin 'iris' ('rainbow'), for the vividly colored salts it forms.
claims.verbatim:
Ir-Iridium is found in igneous rocks at 0.001 ppm,
terrestrial plants at 0.62 ppm and terrestrial animals at 0.00002
ppm. Iridium is one of the hardest and most corrosion resistant
metals known. It is considered a precious metal similar to
platinum.

The English chemist Smithson Tennant discovered
iridium in 1803, using the same process that led him to the
discovery of osmium; he isolated iridium from the residues of
platinum ores he treated with aqua regia (a mixture of nitric
and hydrochloric acids).

Tennant named the new metal iridium after the Latin
word, iris, which translates to “rainbow” because of the highly
colored salts.

claims.claim_text: Where potassium is found in nature. Wallach lists typical concentrations (in parts per million, ppm) across rocks, water, soil, plants and animals — it is a major exchangeable cation (positively charged mineral) in all soils, especially alkaline ones, is concentrated heavily by marine plants (52,000 ppm), and in land animals collects highest in the soft tissue.
claims.verbatim:
K-Potassium is found in igneous rocks at 20,000 ppm,
shale at 26,000 ppm, sandstone at 10,700 ppm, limestone at
2,700 ppm, fresh water at 2.3 ppm, sea water at 380 ppm, soil
at 14,000 ppm (a major exchangeable cation in all soils, but
in highest amounts in alkaline soils), marine plants at 52,000
ppm, terrestrial plants at 14,000 ppm, marine animals at 5,000
to 30,000 ppm, and terrestrial animals at 7,400 ppm (highest
levels are found in soft tissue).

claims.claim_text: What potassium is, chemically. It is a silver-white metal so soft it can easily be cut with a knife, and a member of the alkali-metal family alongside lithium and sodium — like them, it is never found as a pure metal in nature. It was first isolated by Sir Humphrey Davy in 1807 using electrolysis (passing an electric current to split it out of its compounds).
claims.verbatim:
Potassium is a silver-white metal with a characteristic
putty or wax-like nature that is so soft that it can easily be cut
with a knife. It is a member of the family of alkali metals along
with the elements lithium and sodium, and like them is never
found as a pure metal in nature.

claims.claim_text: Potassium carries a natural radioactive isotope. Potassium-40 has a half-life of 1.25 billion years (the time for half of it to decay) and is used to date rocks — as it decays it becomes the noble gas argon, and measuring the argon has dated the oldest rocks on earth to 3.8 billion years. The human body holds about 140 grams of potassium, and since 0.012% of natural potassium is potassium-40, we each carry a small amount — a natural, life-long contributor to our background radiation.
claims.verbatim:
A naturally occurring radioactive isotope of potassium
is potassium-40, which has a half-life of 1.25 billion years.
Potassium-40 is used to date rocks. When potassium-40
decays, it becomes the noble gas argon. To determine the age
of a rock, it is necessary to know how much argon is present
in the rock. The oldest rocks on earth have been dated by this
method as being 3.8 billion years old.

The human body contains approximately 140 grams of
potassium and since the natural level of potassium-40 is 0.012
percent, we all contain small amounts of this isotope - it is a
natural and life-long contributor to our background radiation
load.

claims.claim_text: Potassium, plants, and the origin of its name. Almost all mined potassium chloride goes to plant fertilizer, and plants were humans' early source of the mineral — wood and plants were burned to make a potassium-rich ash called 'potash,' which is where the name potassium comes from. Notably, potassium is essential for plant growth while sodium is not, so plants preferentially take up potassium and let dissolved sodium wash to the oceans. The first 'chemical fertilizer' (NPK — nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) was formulated in the 1700s by the German chemist Liebig.
claims.verbatim:
Almost all of the potassium chloride that is mined is
used as plant fertilizer. In fact, plants (crops and trees) were
the early source of essential minerals including potassium for
humans. Wood and other plants were burned in pots or under
pots to produce a potassium-rich ash (“potash”).

The original “chemical fertilizer,” first produced in the
1700s by the German chemist Liebig, was made up of NPK
(nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) which he formulated
after the ash he produced by burning bread and then analyzing
the mineral content of the ash.

The name, potassium, has its origin from the term
potash, from the early source of the element - wood ashes, the
byproduct of daily living, that was produced by heating and
cooking with wood.

claims.claim_text: Saltpeter — the historic potassium compound. Potassium nitrate (KNO3), commonly called 'saltpeter' or 'rocksalt' (from the Greek 'petra,' rock), looks and tastes like table salt and has been used for centuries as a preservative and fertilizer. It is also one of the three ingredients of gunpowder, along with charcoal and sulfur.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium nitrate, KNO3, is an important compound
that has been used by many cultures for centuries. It is
commonly called “saltpeter” or “rocksalt.” The name is taken
from the Greek word petra, which translates to rock. It looks
like table salt and when dissolved in water, it tastes like salt.

Saltpeter is commonly used as a preservative and
fertilizer. Gunpowder is a mixture of saltpeter, charcoal and
sulfur.

claims.claim_text: What potassium does in the body. It is essential to all organisms and the major cation (positively charged mineral) inside the cell, driving a wide range of electrochemical and enzyme functions. Potassium makes up 5% of the body's total mineral content and is the main mineral of the intracellular fluid (the fluid inside cells). Working with sodium — the other main 'electrolyte' — it maintains normal water balance, osmotic equilibrium (fluid balance across cell membranes), and acid-base (pH) balance; and working with calcium it regulates neuromuscular activity (nerve-and-muscle signaling).
claims.verbatim:
Potassium is essential to all organisms and is the major
cation in cell cytoplasm with a wide variety of electrochemical
and catalytic functions for enzyme systems. Potassium
constitutes five percent of the total mineral content of the
body. It is the major cation of the intracellular fluid and there
is a small amount in the extracellular fluid. With sodium, the
other “electrolyte,” potassium participates in the maintenance
of normal water balance, osmotic equilibrium and acid-base
balance. Potassium participates with calcium in the regulation
of neuromuscular activity.

claims.claim_text: How much potassium the body needs daily. Potassium is easily absorbed, but 90% of what you take in is excreted in the urine and the body stores essentially none — so it must be replaced constantly, requiring a significant daily intake of 5,000 mg (5 grams). This is Wallach's stated daily requirement for potassium.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium is easily absorbed. Ninety percent of ingested
potassium is excreted through the urine. Essentially there is
no storage of potassium in the human body, thus requiring a
significant daily intake of 5,000 mg.

dose.for_condition: daily maintenance intake (body stores no potassium)

claims.claim_text: Signs of a potassium deficiency. Muscular weakness and mental apathy (listlessness, lack of interest) are its features, and hypokalemic cardiac failure — heart failure from low potassium — is the most serious event. Wallach warns that potassium (and other minerals) is lost faster than normal through diuretics (both natural and prescribed water pills), water toxicity (over-drinking water), sweating, colds and flu, vomiting, and diarrhea.
claims.verbatim:
Muscular weakness and mental apathy are features
of a potassium deficiency. Hypokalemic cardiac failure is
the most serious potassium deficiency event. Diuretics (both
natural and prescribed), water toxicity (over drinking water),
sweating, colds and flu, vomiting and diarrhea increase
the rate of loss of all minerals, including potassium, when
compared to the normal expected excretion rate.

claims.claim_text: Krypton — the noble gas of Superman fame. Famous as Superman's home planet and the source of 'kryptonite,' real krypton is a noble gas (an extremely unreactive element) that is totally harmless to humans. Notably, Wallach adds that krypton 'may in fact be an essential element for all vertebrates' — a speculative but intriguing note that even this inert gas could have a biological role.
claims.verbatim:
Kr-Krypton is found in igneous rock at 0.0001 ppm
and sea water at 0.0025 ppm. Krypton is legendary as the
home planet of “Superman” and the source of the mineral
“kryptonite” which had a crippling effect on “Superman.”
In fact krypton in its natural elemental form is a noble gas,
totally harmless to humans and may in fact be an essential
element for all vertebrates.

claims.claim_text: How krypton was discovered. When Mendeleyev built the first periodic table in 1869, no noble gases were yet known, so he left no place for them; the discovery of argon in 1894 forced a whole new column. In 1898 the English chemist Sir William Ramsay isolated and identified krypton, naming it from the Greek 'kryptos' meaning 'hidden.'
claims.verbatim:
As none of the Noble gases had been discovered when
Mendeleyev first constructed the periodic table in 1869, he
made no provision for them in the original table. It was only
the discovery of argon in 1894 that produced the need for a new
column in the table. In 1898, the English chemist Sir William
Ramsay isolated and identified krypton as a new element.
He named it for the Greek word kryptos, which translates to
“hidden.”

claims.claim_text: Krypton's supposed inertness, challenged and broken. The celebrated American chemist and two-time Nobel laureate Linus Pauling used quantum mechanics in 1933 to demonstrate that a molecule containing krypton and fluorine should be stable enough to exist. He was proven right in 1966 when Neil Bartlett of the University of British Columbia produced krypton fluoride (KrF2).
claims.verbatim:
The chemical inertness of krypton was challenged by
the celebrated American chemist and two time Nobel Prize
winner, Linus Pauling, who in 1933 used quantum mechanics
to demonstrate that a molecule containing krypton and
fluorine should be stable enough to exist. In 1966, Neil Bartlett
of the University of British Columbia produced krypton
fluoride (KrF2) as Pauling had predicted.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's theory linking lanthanum to chronic fatigue. The yeast Candida albicans accumulates lanthanum at 370 ppm (parts per million) per day; Wallach theorizes this is how C. albicans produces a debilitating, energy-sapping 'chronic fatigue' disease -- by 'stealing' lanthanum from its victim. He also notes lanthanum's biological potency: at just 0.32 ppm it stimulates the growth of the protozoa Blepherisma and Tetrahymena pyriformis and doubles their lifespan.
claims.verbatim:
Notably the yeast Candida albicans accumulates
lanthanum at the rate of 370 ppm/day. It is theorized that
this is how C. albicans produces a debilitating, energy sapping
“chronic fatigue” disease, by “stealing” lanthanum from the
victim.

The growth of the protozoa Blepherisma and Tetrahymena
pyriformis is stimulated and their life span doubled by the
presence of the rare earth lanthanum at concentrations of 0.32
ppm.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's lithium supplement dose. Chelated lithium supplemented at 1,000-2,000 mcg (1-2 mg) per day produces a dose-related rise in hair-lithium levels -- climbing after four weeks, leveling off by three months, and falling back to baseline within two months of stopping. Wallach notes this response is not seen with metallic lithium carbonate.
claims.verbatim:
Chelated lithium supplemented at 1,000 to 2,000 ug/day causes a dose related increase in hair lithium levels. Hair
lithium levels increased after four weeks of supplementation
and leveled off and became stationary after three months.
When the lithium supplementation was stopped, hair lithium
levels dropped to presupplement values in two months. This
scenario is not seen with the supplementation of metallic
lithium carbonate.

claims.claim_text: Lithium deficiency and mental/behavioral health. Wallach frames depression and manic-depression (bipolar disorder) as, at root, a lithium deficiency aggravated by high sugar -- noting conventional psychiatry itself treats depression with the trace mineral lithium, and lithium carbonate is standard for severe bipolar disorder. He lists depression, manic-depression, hyperactivity, attention-deficit disorders (ADD/ADHD), certain forms of autism, and a spectrum of aggression, rage, and violent or criminal behavior as hallmarks of a lithium deficiency worsened by high sugar or alcohol intake.
claims.verbatim:
In humans, manic depression, depression, “bi-polar”
disease, rage, road rage, “going postal,” Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde
behavior, hyperactivity, ADD, ADHD, certain forms of autism
and “bad seeds” are all hallmarks of a lithium deficiency
aggravated by a high sugar or alcohol intake.

claims.claim_text: Animal studies, Wallach reports, show that a lithium deficiency causes reproductive failure and infertility, slowed growth, a shortened life expectancy, and behavioral problems. He builds on this to argue lithium is a genuine essential trace mineral for the brain — tying its shortage in people (worsened by heavy sugar or alcohol) to depression, manic-depression, and outbursts of rage, the very condition treated with lithium carbonate as a bipolar drug.
claims.verbatim:
Animal studies show that a deficiency of lithium
results in reproductive failure, infertility, reduced growth
rate, shortened life expectancy, and behavioral problems.

claims.claim_text: Lithium levels track with violent and criminal behavior. Wallach reports that normal controls had almost 400 times more hair lithium than violent criminals sampled across California, Florida, Texas, and Oregon -- evidence he ties to lithium's role in curbing aggression and criminal behavior. He cautions that the daily lithium intake estimated by the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency), 650-3,100 mcg, overstates what is usable, since much dietary lithium is metallic and not necessarily bioavailable.
claims.verbatim:
Normal controls showed almost 400 times more hair
lithium than do the violent criminals from California, Florida,
Texas and Oregon. The EPA estimated daily intake of lithium
ranges from 650 to 3,100 ug/day, however, much of the
ingested lithium is metallic and not necessarily biologically
available.

claims.claim_text: Lutetium, a rare-earth element. As the last lanthanide in the periodic table, lutetium is the hardest, heaviest, and one of the least abundant of the rare earths -- silvery-white and corrosion-resistant. It was discovered in 1907 by the Austrian mineralogist Carl Auer von Welsbach and the French scientist Georges Urbain, and named for Lutetia, the ancient name of Paris.
claims.verbatim:
As with most of the other rare earth metals, lutetium
is silvery-white and corrosion-resistant. As the last lanthanide
in the periodic table, it is the hardest and heaviest rare earth
element.

Lutetium is one of the least abundant of the rare
earth elements. It was discovered in 1907 by the Austrian
mineralogist Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach and the French
scientist Georges Urbain as an impurity in a mineral sample
thought to contain ytterbium.

claims.claim_text: Magnesium deficiency diseases. Wallach lists the conditions that flow from a magnesium deficiency: asthma, anorexia, menstrual migraines, growth failure, ECG (electrocardiogram, a heart tracing) changes, neuromuscular problems, tetany (convulsions with muscle cramping), depression, muscular weakness, tremors, and vertigo -- plus calcification of the arterial wall and 'malignant calcification' of soft tissue.

Magnesium Deficiency Diseases

Asthma
Anorexia

Menstrual migraines


 

Growth failure

ECG changes

Neuromuscular problems

Tetany (convulsions with muscle cramping)
Depression

Muscular weakness

Muscle “ties”

Calcification of arterial media

“Malignant calcification” of soft tissue

claims.claim_text: Magnesium deficiency, not cholesterol, as the root of arterial calcification. Wallach calls 'malignant calcification' -- calcium deposits in soft tissue, especially the middle layer (media) of the artery wall -- perhaps the most important manifestation of magnesium deficiency today. He argues magnesium deficiency, not elevated cholesterol or triglycerides, is the basic root cause of the calcium deposits that harden the arteries.
claims.verbatim:
Perhaps the most important manifestation of
magnesium deficiency in modern times is “malignant
calcification.” Malignant calcification appears as calcium
deposits in soft tissue, especially the media or middle layer of
arterial walls. Magnesium deficiency appears to be the basic
root cause of arteriosclerotic calcium deposits, not elevated
blood cholesterol or triglycerides!

claims.claim_text: Calcium and magnesium balance each other. In normal muscle contraction they play antagonistic roles -- calcium the stimulator, magnesium the 'relaxer.' Wallach warns that an excessive amount of calcium can itself induce the signs of a magnesium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium and magnesium have antagonistic roles in
normal muscle contraction, calcium acting as the stimulator
and magnesium as the “relaxer.” An excessive amount of
calcium can induce signs of magnesium deficiency.

claims.claim_text: What magnesium does -- and what too much does. Magnesium is required for producing and transferring energy, for protein synthesis, for muscle contractility and nerve excitability, and as a cofactor in a myriad of enzyme systems. Wallach also warns (his emphasis) that an excess of magnesium will cause diarrhea and inhibit bone calcification.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium is required for the production and transfer
of energy for protein synthesis, for contractility of muscle and
excitability of nerves, and as a cofactor in a myriad of enzyme
systems. AN EXCESS OF MAGNESIUM WILL CAUSE
DIARRHEA AND INHIBIT BONE CALCIFICATION.

claims.claim_text: Magnesium as the 'ultimate source of all biological energy.' Magnesium is the metal atom found in the chlorophyll of every green plant, driving photosynthesis -- the process that stores the sun's energy as the chemical 'solar currency' feeding all plants, animals, and humans. Wallach calls magnesium, the source of the deep green of plants, the ultimate source of all biological energy.
claims.verbatim:
It is also the metallic atom found in
chlorophyll of all green plants, which plays an essential role
in photosynthesis, the photochemical process that converts the
sun’s solar energy into a stored “solar currency” for a source
of chemical energy for all plants and all animals and humans.
Magnesium, the source of the deep green color of plants, is the
ultimate source of all biological energy!

claims.claim_text: How well magnesium is absorbed. Absorption ranges from 24% to 85%: metallic sources of magnesium are absorbed least, and plant-derived colloidal mineral sources most. Vitamin D has no effect on magnesium absorption; dietary fat, phytates, and calcium reduce it; and high-performance athletes lose a considerable amount of magnesium in sweat.
claims.verbatim:
The rate of absorption of magnesium ranges from 24
to 85%. The lesser absorption rate is for metallic sources of
Mg, the higher rates of absorption are associated with plant
derived colloidal mineral sources. Vitamin D has no effect
on Mg absorption. The presence of dietary fat, phytates, and
calcium reduces the efficiency of absorption. High performance
athletes lose a considerable amount of Mg in sweat.

claims.claim_text: Magnesium's reference intake and safety ceiling. Wallach cites the RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) -- 350 mg/day for adult men, 300 mg/day for women, and 450 mg/day for pregnant and lactating women -- and notes that, with healthy kidneys, there is no evidence of toxicity even at supplemental doses up to 6,000 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
The RDA for Mg is 350 mg/day for adult males, 300
mg/day for adult females, and 450 mg/day for pregnant and
lactating females. If the kidneys are healthy, there is no evidence
of toxicity at supplemental doses of up to 6,000 mg/day.

claims.claim_text: Wallach attributes Keshan disease (KSD) to a selenium deficiency. Named for Keshan Province, China, where selenium-poor soil made it endemic, the disease is a cardiomyopathy — a degeneration of the heart muscle that Wallach classes as a form of muscular dystrophy of the heart (also called 'mulberry heart disease'). He notes the World Health Organization tied the Chinese cardiomyopathy to the selenium deficiency of the local soil, and that large-scale double-blind supplementation trials confirmed selenium deficiency as the cause — supplementing children with selenium sharply cut the disease rate.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in
communities living at a distance from the sea; Keshan disease
(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.claim_text: Wallach identifies cardiomyopathy — degeneration of the heart muscle — as a selenium deficiency disease. He equates it with Keshan disease and 'mulberry heart disease' (a heart muscular dystrophy), and points to the WHO's finding that the cardiomyopathy of Chinese children in Keshan Province was caused by the selenium deficiency of the local soil. In his view the same deficiency underlies cardiomyopathy generally — he cites it as what killed running author Jim Fixx ('a simple selenium deficiency disease') — and he holds that inexpensive selenium supplementation can prevent it and, in its early phases, even clinically cure it.

claims.claim_text: Wallach teaches that pica is fundamentally a mineral-deficiency behavior. He describes it as a seeking or craving — with licking, chewing, and the eating of bizarre non-food substances — that has its genesis in mineral deficiencies, and he is emphatic that neither vitamin, protein, nor calorie deficiency triggers it, and that eating sugar, carbohydrate, fat, or protein will not quench it. The body is hunting for the minerals it lacks. In his survey of regional mineral-deficiency diseases, Wallach attributes the phosphate (phosphorus) deficiency form of pica specifically to South Africa.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to Australia as the classic home of copper-deficiency disease. Enzootic ataxia — a copper deficiency — was a common disease of Australian lambs and adult sheep from the late 19th century; it was first scientifically described in the Australian veterinary journals in 1932 and reported across Western Australia, South Australia, and Victoria. The disease is characterized by poor coordination, weakness, and demyelinating lesions in the spinal cord.

Iodine deficiency (goiter) occurred in

(cardiomyopathy) caused by a selenium deficiency occurred
in Keshan Province, China; phosphate deficiency (pica) was
common in South Africa; copper deficiency (enzootic ataxia)
was common in Australia, etc.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that phytates are phytic acid — chemically inositol hexaphosphate — found abundantly in whole grains and raw vegetables, and that this same compound interferes with the absorption of calcium, iron, zinc and other nutrients, making it a required nutrient on one hand and a dietary negative on the other.
claims.verbatim:
It
occurs abundantly in diets containing whole grains and
raw vegetables as inositol phospholipids and as phytic acid
(inositol hexaphosphate or “phytates”).


 

Phytic acid interferes with the absorption of calcium,
iron, zinc and other nutrients - on one hand a required nutrient
and on the other a negative in the diet.

claims.claim_text: Because phytate/high-phosphorus foods block calcium and make the ideal 2:1 calcium-to-phosphorus ratio unreachable from food alone, Wallach's practical answer is to avoid high-phosphorus foods such as raw vegetables (phytates) and colas as much as possible, and supplement instead with highly absorbable plant-derived colloidal and chelated calcium.
claims.verbatim:
The only
possible way to approach the 2:1 ideal is to avoid as much as
possible the food items containing high levels of phosphorous
(i.e. - raw vegetables (phytates), colas, etc.) and supplement
with plant derived colloidal and chelated calcium.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that heavy intake of sugar, carbonation, and caffeine (from coffee, tea, colas) works against calcium two ways at once: it lowers how efficiently calcium is absorbed AND pulls stored calcium back out of the bones.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of sugar, carbonation and
caffeine from coffee, tea, colas, etc. will reduce the efficiency
of absorption and will leach stored calcium from the bones.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin in the gut and blocks its absorption -- it takes 24 raw egg whites to create a biotin deficiency, which is an argument for cooking eggs rather than eating whites raw.
claims.verbatim:
Originally biotin deficiency was
observed in chicks and rats that were fed raw egg whites, which
it was learned later, contained an “egg-white-injury” factor.

Avidin, a material found in egg white, combines with
biotin in the intestine making it unavailable for absorption.
It takes 24 raw egg whites to contribute enough avidin to
create a biotin deficiency in humans.

claims.claim_text: Wallach lists fresh whole milk, eggs, cheese and muscle meats (along with liver and kidney) as rich sources of vitamin B12, and warns that pasteurized and evaporated milk have lost 40 to 90 percent of their B12.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is found in liver, kidney, fresh whole milk,
eggs, cheese and muscle meats are rich sources. Pasteurized
and evaporated milk have lost 40 to 90% of vitamin B12.

claims.claim_text: Wallach flips the conventional wisdom: the hydrogenated and partially-hydrogenated vegetable oils (margarine) once sold as the safe substitute for butter to prevent arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and stroke are now known to directly CAUSE those very diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated vegetable
oils, once touted by the medical trade as a safe substitute for
butter in the prevention of arteriosclerosis, atherosclerosis and
stroke, are now known to be the direct cause of these diseases.

claims.claim_text: Wallach flatly rejects the vegan line — he says red meat is healthy and that every long-lived population on earth eats it. In his words, all long-lived peoples eat red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), plus poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, and vegans 'lie to themselves' when they insist the world's healthiest people avoid animal products. His warning is concrete: strict vegans who don't supplement minerals correctly tend, within 5 years, to develop grey hair, receding gums, periodontal disease, arthritis, osteoporosis, anemia, hypertension, chronic fatigue, even cancer and liver cirrhosis — because an unsupplemented plant diet leaves them 51 to 57 of the body's essential minerals short (plants can't manufacture minerals). In his words: "all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy"
claims.verbatim:
Vegans as a group tend to lie to themselves and
convince themselves (and try to convince others) that all of
the long-lived people on earth do not eat animal products. In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

His core claim: every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and no vegan, he says, has ever lived to 100 or raised a thriving colony of healthy kids on the diet. Unsupplemented strict vegans, he warns, tend to develop grey hair, receding gums, osteoporosis, anemia, arthritis and even cancer within 5 years, and he points to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who died at 56 of breast cancer.
claims.verbatim:
Vegans as a group tend to lie to themselves and
convince themselves (and try to convince others) that all of
the long-lived people on earth do not eat animal products. In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

claims.claim_text: Wallach groups commercial FRIED chicken with French fries, fried seafood, high-fructose corn syrup, soft drinks and white flour as things the world's longest-lived Blue Zone peoples simply have no access to — framing the frying and processing, not the chicken itself, as the food of ill health.
claims.verbatim:
One of the unintended benefits of the Blues Zones is
that they are remote and have little or no access to doctors,
pharmaceuticals, commercial French fries, fried chicken, fried
fish, fried shrimp, fried clams, high fructose corn syrup, soft
drinks, white flour, etc.

claims.claim_text: Wallach offers a kitchen demonstration that bone's calcium sits in a crystal structure bound to a protein framework: put a chicken drumstick bone in a quart of vinegar for 2 weeks and the calcium is leached out, leaving the protein matrix behind.
claims.verbatim:
To extract the calcium from a bone and reveal the
protein matrix, put a chicken “drumstick” bone in a quart of
vinegar for two weeks and the calcium will be leached out of
the bone leaving the protein matrix.

claims.claim_text: Wallach uses poultry as the model: arsenic plus the B-vitamin choline prevents 100% of perosis ('slipped tendon') in chickens, and the same arsenic deficiency in humans shows up as carpal tunnel syndrome, temporomandibular jaw-joint pain (TMJ) and other repetitive-motion joint diseases.
claims.verbatim:
Arsenic in combination with the B-vitamin choline
prevents 100% of perosis (“slipped tendon”) in poultry. Arsenic
deficiency in humans results in a “carpal tunnel syndrome,”
“TMJ,” and other “repetitive motion” type degenerative joint
diseases and minute traces stimulate the production of red
blood cells.

claims.claim_text: Relaying Taoist Chinese tradition, Wallach notes that under the Tao the heart is related to fire, the lungs to metal and the kidneys to water, and that poultry, vegetables and fish are held to nourish these organs.
claims.verbatim:
According to the Tao, the heart is related to
fire, the lungs to metal, the kidneys to water and foods that
nourish these organs include poultry, vegetables and fish.

claims.claim_text: Wallach defines a 'pollo-vegetarian' as really an omnivore who eats poultry on top of grains, vegetables, fruit and nuts — part of his point that most self-described vegetarians actually eat animal foods.
claims.verbatim:
Pollo-vegetarians - omnivores, who, eat poultry in
addition to grains vegetables, fruit and nuts.

claims.claim_text: Wallach classes pork as a red meat and notes that every long-lived people on earth eats it, so pork counts as legitimate animal protein rather than something to shun.

In
fact all long lived peoples on earth eat red meat (including
pork, beef, goat, lamb, etc.), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy.

claims.claim_text: Wallach lists eggs among the rich dietary sources of vitamin B12, alongside liver, kidney, whole milk, cheese, and muscle meats, which matters because vegans risk B12 deficiency without such foods.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is found in liver, kidney, fresh whole milk,
eggs, cheese and muscle meats are rich sources.

claims.claim_text: Wallach calls cobalt's essentiality unusual: what the body requires is not cobalt on its own but a cobalt COMPLEX — the molecule cyanocobalamine, better known as vitamin B12. A requirement for pure cobalt, he says, is found only in some bacteria and algae. The need for B12 cobalt, he notes, is thought by some to represent a symbiosis: microbes build B12 out of elemental cobalt, and vertebrates — us — require the finished B12.
claims.verbatim:
The essentiality
of cobalt is unusual in that the requirement is for a cobalt

complex known as cyanocobalamine or vitamin B12. A pure
cobalt requirement is only found in some bacteria and algae
and the need for B12 cobalt is thought by some to represent a
symbiotic relationship between microbes which generate and
manufacture B12 from elemental cobalt and vertebrates that
require B12.

claims.claim_text: A public figure Wallach points to for the liquid supplement. Nelson Mandela was mentally sharp and physically animated at his 90th birthday in 2008 — remarkable, Wallach notes, after 27 years in a South African prison on a very low-calorie, protein-restricted diet. On his release, Mandela began drinking South African wine for its antioxidants and taking a liquid form of plant-derived minerals, sent to him from Atlanta by former UN Ambassador Andrew Young.
claims.verbatim:
Immediately upon release from prison Mandela began
to drink South African wine (a significant source of resveratrol
and polyphenols - antioxidants) and supplement with a liquid
form of plant derived minerals shipped to him from Atlanta,
Georgia by former UN Ambassador Andrew Young.

claims.claim_text: ORAC stands for Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity. Wallach calls it the universally agreed method of predicting the antioxidant power and free-radical neutralising value of foods, drink and supplements. Because it puts all three on one scale, he can set a daily point target rather than simply telling people to eat more vegetables.
claims.verbatim: ORAC is a method of measuring antioxidant capacities of various foods.

claims.claim_text: The ORAC test is a government-developed metric, not a supplement-industry one. It was created by scientists at the National Institute on Aging, a division of the NIH in Baltimore, working with Tufts University in Boston. The USDA went on to publish ORAC values for 277 commonly eaten foods in 2007 and a full database in 2008.
claims.verbatim:
It was developed
by scientists at the National Institute on Aging, a division of the National Institute
of Health (NIH) in Baltimore, Maryland and Tufts University, Boston, Massachusetts.

claims.claim_text: The ORAC assay puts a fluorescent dye in a tube with peroxyl radicals that destroy it, and scores how well a food protects that dye. The peroxyl radical is chosen deliberately: it is one of the most common reactive oxygen species found in the human body, so the test measures defence against damage that actually happens in you rather than an abstract laboratory reaction.
claims.verbatim:
The ORAC analysis, which utilizes Florescein as the florescent probe, provides a
measure of the scavenging capacity of antioxidants against the peroxyl radical, which
is one of the most common reactive oxygen species (ROS) found in the body.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's daily target is 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points, which he gives as the optimal intake for reaching the age of 100. It is a maintenance figure, not a cure, and he never presents it alone: in the same book he pairs it with cutting free-radical foods such as fried food, trans fats, burnt fat, nitrites, alcohol and sugar, taking every essential nutrient with a special focus on minerals, and a calorie-restricted diet. He is also explicit that antioxidants by themselves raise a population's average lifespan but not its maximum.
claims.verbatim:
A universally agreed upon method of predicting the antioxidant power and free radical
neutralizing value of foods, drink and supplements is the Oxygen Radical Absorbance
Capacity or ORAC value - based on current studies, we believe that the optimal total
daily intake of ORAC points to reach the age of 100 years is 20,000 to 25,000 per day.

claims.claim_text: The published ORAC numbers come from the USDA, which released an updated list of values for 277 commonly consumed American foods in 2007 and a full database in 2008. The list spans fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, spices, grains and drinks. What interests Wallach is the pattern it exposed: the correlation between high-antioxidant fruits and vegetables and better health outcomes is what ties the metric back to the free-radical theory of aging.
claims.verbatim:
In 2007, scientists with the USDA published an updated list of ORAC values for 277
foods commonly consumed by the U.S. population (fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds,

The damage runs in steps: they attack polyunsaturated fats and cholesterol in cell membranes, producing lipid peroxides, which decompose into aldehydes that cross-link proteins, lipids and DNA. So in his framework, getting the benefit of antioxidants is inseparable from getting the minerals that power them, and he measures the antioxidant strength of foods by their ORAC score.

The antagonism runs both directions (mercury, in turn, protects against selenium overdose), but the practical upshot is that he treats adequate selenium as a frontline defense for anyone carrying mercury fillings or exposed to environmental mercury.

An adult body holds 20 to 28 grams of magnesium, most of it locked in bone and skeletal muscle. About half of the body's magnesium — most of it bound in bone — is not exchangeable, meaning it can't be readily called on when you run short.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that pure ascorbic acid was first isolated in 1928 by Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, who found it in adrenal tissue, orange and cabbage and called it hexuronic acid. It was not until 1932 that C. Glenn King, at the University of Pittsburgh, reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons and identified it as vitamin C, showing it had the properties of preventing and curing scurvy in guinea pigs.
claims.verbatim:
Pure ascorbic acid was isolated in 1928 by Albert
Szent-Gyorgyi, who discovered it in adrenal tissue, orange
and cabbage and identified it as hexuronic acid. It was not
until 1932 that C. Glenn King at the University of Pittsburgh
reisolated ascorbic acid from lemons that it was identified as
vitamin C and had the properties of preventing and curing
scurvy in guinea pigs.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, British sailors were often called 'limeys' because they carried lemons - not limes - on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy, the vitamin C deficiency disease. The vitamin C in the citrus kept crews from developing scurvy on long voyages.
claims.verbatim:
British sailors
were oftentimes referred to as “limeys” because they carried
lemons (not limes) on their ships to prevent and cure scurvy.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin, absorbed along with the ordinary dietary fats in a meal and stored mainly in the body's fat. Because of this, any health problem or habit that interferes with fat absorption also interferes with vitamin A absorption and function — Wallach names antibiotic use, gallbladder disease, celiac disease, dietary fat deficiencies, high-fiber diets, and taking mineral oil with meals.
claims.verbatim:
The fat soluble vitamins are absorbed along with other
common and essential dietary lipids and any health challenge
or health practice that interferes with the absorption of fats
(antibiotic use, gall bladder disease, celiac disease, dietary
fat deficiencies, high fiber diets, mineral oil
consumption during meals and overt deficiencies) interferes
with fat soluble vitamin absorption and function.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin A comes both preformed in animal foods and as carotenoids in plants. The book's food table lists beef liver highest by far (about 43,900 units per 100 g), then raw carrots (11,000), baked sweet potato (8,100), cooked spinach (7,300), and dried apricots (5,500). Wallach notes vegetables carry vitamin A activity in proportion to their carotenoid content — carotene, cryptoxanthin, and other yellow, red, or orange pigments that are often hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.
claims.verbatim:
Vegetables were later found to contain vitamin A
activity in relation to their carotenoid content - carotene,
cryptoxanthin and other yellow, red or orange pigments that
were oftentimes hidden by the green pigment of chlorophyll.

claims.claim_text: Investigators noticed that animals kept longer on fat-free diets developed inflammation and infections of the eyes — problems that were quickly reversed when fats from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet. In 1924 the Danish investigator Bloch showed that xerophthalmia (dry, damaged eyes) in children was the same disease described in laboratory rats in 1913, and that it could be prevented or cured by adding liver, butter, or cod liver oil to the diet.
claims.verbatim:
Investigators also noted that those animals that lived
longer on fat free diets developed inflammation and infections
of the eyes - these conditions were quickly rever sed when fats
from butter or cod liver oil were added to the diet.

In 1924, Bloch, showed that
xerophthalmia in children was the same disease described in
1913 in laboratory rats, and that the disease could be prevented
or cured by adding liver, butter or cod liver oil to their diet.

claims.claim_text: Wallach lists vitamin D's core functions as stimulating the active, energy-requiring intestinal absorption of calcium and the active phosphate-transport system in the intestine. Working with parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium from bone to maintain normal blood calcium levels, and it mobilizes phosphate from bone to maintain proper serum phosphate levels. It also supports the kidney's reabsorption of calcium from urine. In short, vitamin D governs how the body handles calcium and phosphorus.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin D Functions:

Stimulates the active, intestinal

absorption of calcium.

energy requiring

Stimulates the active phosphate-transport system in
the intestine.

With the parathyroid hormone, it mobilizes calcium
from bone to maintain normal blood levels of calcium.

It mobilizes phosphate from the bone to maintain
proper serum phosphate levels.

It supports reabsorption of calcium from urine by the
kidney.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa into 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), and that the skin and other tissues also carry out this process when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight. Separately, ergosterol, a yeast sterol, is converted into vitamin D2 on exposure to sunlight or UV light. This is why sun exposure is a primary source of vitamin D and why cholesterol is its raw material.
claims.verbatim:
Ergosterol, a yeast
sterol, is converted to vitamin D2 when exposed to ultraviolet
light. Cholesterol is converted by the intestinal mucosa
to 7-dehydrocholesterol, the provitamin of vitamin D3,
cholecalciferol. This process is also carried out by the skin and
other tissues, when exposed to ultraviolet light and sunlight.

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites Dr. Michael Holick of Boston University, who said the bottom line is that vitamin D is important for the health of both children and adults and may help prevent many serious chronic diseases. He reports Holick's finding that vitamin D deficiency in adults increases the risk of heart attacks, increases mortality in breast and colon cancer victims, raises mortality in dialysis patients, and increases the risk of type II diabetes in children. This positions vitamin D as protective against major chronic diseases, not just rickets.
claims.verbatim:
In 2006 Dr. Michael Holick, a professor of medicine,
physiology and biophysics at Boston University said, “The
bottom line is, we now recognize that vitamin D, is important
for health for both children and adults and may help prevent
many serious chronic diseases.”
Holick’s studies have shown that deficiencies of
vitamin D, in adults results in an increase in risk of heart

attacks, increased mortality in breast and colon cancer


 

victims, increased risk of mortality in dialysis patients and an
increased risk of developing type II diabetes in children.

claims.claim_text: Not all dietary iron is equal, Wallach explains: heme iron from meat is about 10% absorbable, while iron from fresh plant sources is only about 1% available, because the plants' own phytates lock it up. Absorption happens mainly in the duodenum — the first stretch of the small intestine, where the contents are still acidic — which is one reason low stomach acid worsens iron status. It underlies his caution that vegetarians are especially prone to iron deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Iron is stored in bone marrow and liver (i.e. hemosiderin
and ferritin). Heme iron from meat is 10% available for
absorption, while iron from fresh plant sources are only one
percent available because of the endogenous phytates in the
plant. Iron absorption takes place primarily in the duodenum
where the intestinal environment is still acid.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum while the environment is still acid, and the absorption rate falls once the intestinal contents turn alkaline. It is taken up by active cellular transport and simple diffusion, but metallic calcium absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and is easily disrupted by other substances in the gut. Under ideal conditions calcium is highly absorbable — up to 98% in the organically bound, plant-derived colloidal and water-soluble chelated forms.
claims.verbatim:
Calcium is primarily absorbed in the duodenum, where
the environment is still acid. Once the food in the intestine
converts to an alkaline pH, the absorption rate of calcium will
decline. Calcium is absorbed from the small intestine by active
cellular transport and by simple diffusion. Metallic calcium
absorption may be limited to one to three percent or less and
can be affected by many substances in the gut. Under ideal
circumstances calcium is highly absorbable, up to 98% in the
organically bound plant derived colloidal mineral and water
soluble chelated form.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that a 1,000 mg calcium carbonate tablet only contains 400 mg of metallic (elemental) calcium, and metallic minerals are only about 8 to 12% absorbable in the young and as little as 3 to 5% after age 35 to 40. So two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules do not deliver 2,000 mg of calcium — they supply 800 mg of elemental calcium, of which roughly 80 mg is actually absorbed. To get 2,000 mg of usable calcium from calcium carbonate, he calculates you would have to take 25 capsules a day, meaning a 100-capsule bottle would last only four days.
claims.verbatim:
A typical metallic mineral supplement, either alone or
part of a multiple is calcium carbonate. Calcium carbonate can
be purchased in 1,000 mg tablets or capsules, which breaks
down to 400 mg of metallic calcium and 600 mg of carbonate.
Two 1,000 mg calcium carbonate capsules or tablets do not
give you 2,000 mg of calcium - they only supply 800 mg of
elemental calcium and at a 10% availability rate you will net
only 80 mg of available calcium. Therefore, to get 2,000 mg of
usable calcium from a 1,000 mg capsule or tablet of calcium
carbonate, you would have to take 25 capsules each day! A
100 capsule bottle of calcium carbonate will therefore only
last 4 days.

claims.claim_text: Wallach notes that in the 1st century the Romans used a calcium compound they called calx, the Latin word for lime -- the root of the modern name. The pure metal itself was first isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy. Calcium is an extremely reactive element that is never found in pure form in nature.
claims.verbatim:
In the 1st century, the Romans used a compound of
calcium they called calx (lime) in Latin.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, mild vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency produces mental confusion, muscular weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness, muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of interest in daily tasks and general lethargy. Chronic deficiency advances to a polyneuritis and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening pulmonary edema. The signs therefore span both the nervous system and the cardiovascular system.
claims.verbatim:
Mild deficiencies produce mental confusion, muscular
weakness, peripheral paralysis, calf muscle tenderness,
muscle fatigue, emotional instability, loss of appetite, loss of
interest in daily tasks and general lethargy.

Chronic deficiencies of thiamine result in a polyneuritis
and congestive heart failure with edema and life-threatening
pulmonary edema.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that fats spare thiamine because they can be metabolized for energy without the need for it, whereas the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine. In practical terms, a diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrate increases the body's demand for vitamin B1. Fats also aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
claims.verbatim:
Fats aid in the transport and absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Fats spare thiamin since they
can be metabolized for energy without the need for thiamin,
whereas, the metabolism of carbohydrate requires thiamine.

claims.claim_text: Where to get riboflavin (vitamin B2): Wallach lists milk, cheddar and cottage cheese, organ meats such as liver, heart, and kidney, eggs, and green leafy vegetables — but only in small amounts, so variety matters. He adds that B2 was first spotted in 1879 as the yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, and that a shortage shows up first as soreness and burning of the lips, mouth, and tongue, along with light-sensitive, itchy eyes.
claims.verbatim:
Riboflavin is present in small amounts in milk, cheddar
and cottage cheese, organ meats (liver, heart, kidney, etc.),
eggs and green leafy vegetables.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that riboflavin (vitamin B2) was recognized in 1879 as a yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey, but its biological significance was not understood until 1932, when a team of German investigators isolated 'Warburg's yellow enzyme' from yeast and demonstrated that the substance was necessary for an intracellular enzyme to function. The substance was synthesized in 1935 by Kuhn, who gave it the name riboflavin.
claims.verbatim:
Riboflavin or vitamin B2 was recognized in 1879 as a
yellow-green fluorescent pigment in milk whey. The biological
significance of this yellow pigment was not understood
until 1932 when a team of German investigators isolated
“Warburg’s yellow enzyme” from yeast and demonstrated
that the substance was necessary for the functioning of an
intracellular enzyme. The substance was synthesized in 1935
by Kuhn and named riboflavin.

claims.claim_text: The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as muscular weakness, anorexia (loss of appetite), indigestion, and skin eruptions. Severe niacin deficiency produces classic pellagra, characterized by the '3 D's' — dermatitis, dementia, and diarrhea — along with tremors and a sore tongue ('beef tongue').
claims.verbatim:
The early stages of niacin deficiency show up as
muscular weakness, anorexia, indigestion and skin eruptions.
Severe deficiency of niacin produces classic pellagra which is
characterized by the “3 D’s” of pellagra (dermatitis, dementia
and diarrhea), tremors and sore tongue or “ beef tongue.”

claims.claim_text: Vitamin B5, also called pantothenic acid, is one of the essential B-complex vitamins. In Wallach's framework it is indispensable because it forms part of coenzyme A, the molecule that runs two-carbon unit metabolism. Through coenzyme A the body requires B5 to metabolize all three major food groups - carbohydrates, lipids (fats), and proteins - which places it at the center of energy production and the manufacture of fatty acids, steroid hormones, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Because it is water-soluble and continuously used up, it must be supplied through diet and daily supplementation; a shortfall shows up as burning feet, dermatitis, fatigue, depression, and a racing heartbeat.
claims.verbatim:
Pantothenic acid or vitamin B. is part of coenzyme A,
which functions in two-carbon unit metabolism. Pantothenic
acid is required for the metabolism of carbohydrates, lipids
and proteins.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes a pyridoxine deficiency syndrome in mentally retarded children who also have convulsions caused by an inborn error of B6 metabolism. These children are thought to be unable to synthesize GABA, and correcting the syndrome requires daily ingestion of large amounts of B6 to prevent permanent retardation. He adds that children with cryptogenic epilepsy appearing at several years of age likewise need large oral doses of B6 to improve the EEG and control seizures.
claims.verbatim:
A deficiency syndrome for pyridoxine has been
identified in mentally retarded children that also have
convulsions due to an inborn error of B6 metabolism. It is
thought that these children are unable to synthesize GABA;
correction of this syndrome requires daily ingestion of large
amounts of B6 to prevent permanent retardation.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that pyridoxine, or vitamin B6, was identified in 1938 as a separate entity within the vitamin 'B-complex.' Rather than a single molecule, B6 is a functional complex of three closely related chemical compounds: pyridoxine, pyridoxamine, and pyridoxal. Together these forms carry out the vitamin's roles in the body.
claims.verbatim:
Pyridoxine or vitamin B6 was identified in 1938 as a
fraction or separate entity of the vitamin “B-complex.” Vitamin
B6 is a functional complex of three closely related chemical
compounds - pyridoxine, pyridoxamine and pyridoxal.

claims.claim_text: In pernicious anemia, which is caused by a vitamin B12 deficiency, folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the corrected blood picture hides the ongoing B12-related nerve and gut damage.
claims.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

claims.claim_text: Folacin, or folic acid, was first identified as one of many growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in the prevention and treatment of anemia; it was synthesized in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for humans. Wallach states that folic acid deficiencies may be the most common vitamin deficiency in humans. The deficiency produces poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, multiple blood disorders, glossitis, and gastrointestinal tract disturbances.
claims.verbatim:
Folacin or folic acid was identified as one of many
growth factors in bacteria and laboratory animals and in
the prevention and treatment of anemia. It was synthesized
in 1946 and quickly established as an essential nutrient for
humans.

Folic acid deficiencies may be the most common

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, vitamin B12 -- also called cobalamin -- is a red, water-soluble vitamin, and both its color and its function trace to a single cobalt atom held at the center of the molecule, which makes B12 the body's main way of using the essential mineral cobalt. It is a fragile compound, slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances, and about 30% of its activity is destroyed during cooking. B12 works together with folic acid to build DNA and RNA, supports the bone marrow in making red blood cells, and is needed to form the myelin that insulates nerves -- so a deficiency shows up as pernicious anemia and progressive nerve damage. Because only bacteria, fungi, and algae can actually manufacture it, B12 reaches people mainly through animal foods and supplements, and absorbing it depends on adequate stomach acid plus an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor.'
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline, water-soluble vitamin, and its red color comes directly from the cobalt atom held inside the molecule. It is a fragile compound, slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. Because of this fragility, roughly 30% of B12's activity is destroyed during cooking, whether by electric, gas, microwave, wood, or charcoal heat.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water
soluble. The red color is due to the cobalt atom in the molecule.
Vitamin B12 is slowly deactivated by exposure to acid, alkali,
light, and oxidizing or reducing substances. About 30% of
B12 activity is lost during cooking (electric, gas, microwave,
wood, charcoal, etc.).

claims.claim_text: For vitamin B12 to be absorbed, the intrinsic factor must be present and the stomach must be acidic, at a pH of 2.0 or less. Intrinsic factor is a mucoprotein enzyme (Castle's intrinsic factor) that is part of normal stomach secretions. When a person has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid, usually from a salt/NaCl deficiency), the intrinsic factor stops working and B12 cannot be absorbed, which is why doctors frequently give B12 shots to older people on salt-restricted diets.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic cobalt itself is absorbed at the rate of 20 to
26.2% by mice and in humans if intrinsic factor is present
in the stomach and the stomach pH is 2.0 or less. Intrinsic
factor is a mucoprotein enzyme known as Castle’s intrinsic
factor and is part of normal stomach secretions. If a person
has hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid- usually a NaCl
deficiency) the intrinsic factor will not work and B12 cobalt is
not absorbed - this is why doctors frequently give B12 shots
to older people on salt restricted diets.

claims.claim_text: In pernicious anemia, which is a B12 deficiency, taking folic acid will produce a marked improvement in the anemia itself. However, the gastrointestinal symptoms and the neurologic lesions continue to progress unchecked. Wallach calls this the 'masking effect' of folic acid, because the visible improvement in the blood hides the ongoing nerve and gastrointestinal damage of untreated B12 deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
In pernicious anemia (B12 deficiency), folic acid will
produce a marked improvement in the anemia, however,
the gastrointestinal symptoms and neurologic lesions will
continue to progress - this is referred to as the “masking
effect” of folic acid.

claims.claim_text: The very first vitamin B12 molecule isolated in the laboratory happened to contain a cyanide group, and that is how it got the name cyanocobalamine. Several different cobalamine compounds carry vitamin B12 activity, but cyanocobalamine and hydroxycobalamine are the most active.
claims.verbatim:
The original B12 molecule isolated
in the laboratory contained a cyanide group, thus the name
cyanocobalamine. There are several different cobalamine
compounds that have B12 activity, with cyanocobalamine and
hydroxycobalamine being the most active.

claims.claim_text: Copper is a genuine essential nutrient -- every living organism needs it. Wallach frames it as a universally important cofactor, the helper mineral that many hundreds of the body's metalloenzymes (enzymes built around a metal atom) depend on to work. Through those enzymes copper builds the pigment in hair and skin, forms the elastic fibers that give tensile strength to blood vessels, skin and vertebral discs, and helps cells use oxygen. He stresses that copper deficiency is widespread and common, and that copper-deficiency diseases have a real, under-recognized impact on human populations -- which is why he ties so many conditions, from gray hair to aneurysms, back to too little copper.
claims.verbatim:
Copper is an essential nutrient for all living organisms
and is a universally important cofactor for many hundreds
of metalloenzymes. Copper deficiency is widespread and
common and copper deficiency diseases have an important
impact on human populations.

claims.claim_text: Wallach groups copper oxide with the metallic minerals such as calcium carbonate, oyster shell and iron oxide. He says metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary, are only 8 to 12 percent biologically available to younger people and drop to just 3 to 5 percent after age 35 to 40, so he treats copper oxide as a poor form of copper compared with plant-derived colloidal minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary
are only 8 to 12% biologically available to younger animals
and humans; after attaining the age of 35 to 40 years, the
availability of metallic minerals for humans plummets to 3 to
5%.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, the radiant colors of many precious gems come from trace amounts of chromium. Small amounts of chromium in the form of corundum give rubies their red color, while the chromium-bearing mineral beryl produces the characteristic green of emeralds.
claims.verbatim:
The beautiful and radiant colors, of many precious gems,
are also due to the presence of trace amounts of chromium.
The red color of rubies is produced by small amounts of
chromium in the form of corundum. The characteristic green
color of emeralds is produced by the presence of the chromium
bearing mineral beryl.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes where chromium occurs in nature, from about 100 ppm in igneous rocks and 90 ppm in shale down to trace levels in fresh and sea water, with soils ranging from 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and serpentine). In living tissue, he notes, chromium accumulates in RNA and insulin.
claims.verbatim:
Cr-Chromium is found in igneous rocks at 100 ppm,
shale at 90 ppm, sandstone at 35 ppm, limestone at 11 ppm,
fresh water at 0.00018 ppm, sea water at 0.00005 ppm, soils
at 5 to 3,000 ppm (highest in soils derived from basalt and
serpentine), marine plants at 1 ppm, terrestrial plants at 0.23
ppm, marine animals at 0.2 to 1.0 ppmand in terrestrial animals
at 0.075 ppm, where it accumulates in RNA and insulin.

claims.claim_text: Wallach highlights a steady decline in the average American serum chromium since 1948. His figures fall from 28 (city) and 1000 (rural) in 1948 to roughly 13 in 1971, down through the 1970s, and to just 0.13 by 1985 — a dramatic collapse in the population's chromium status over a few decades.
claims.verbatim:
Of greater concern has been the steady decline in the
average American serum chromium since 1948.

Mean Chromium Blood Levels (ug/l) Year
28 (city) 1000 (rural) 1948
13 1971
10 1972
4.7-5.1 1973
0.73 - 1.6 1974
0.16 1978
0.43 1980
0.13 1985

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that the balance of sodium, potassium and chloride is regulated by hormones from the adrenal cortex together with the anterior pituitary gland. In Addison's disease — a loss of adrenal-cortex function — the body can no longer retain sodium and potassium properly, producing general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss and a marked 'salt hunger.' He notes these symptoms can be relieved by supplementing salt (NaCl) or by giving adrenal cortical hormones.
claims.verbatim:
Hormonal control of Na, K and Cl balance is regulated
by the adrenal cortex hormones as well as by the anterior
pituitary gland. Addison’s Disease, a loss of function of the
adrenal cortex, results in the loss of Na and K retention with
clinical signs of general weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss,
and a marked “salt hunger.” The symptoms can be relieved
with the supplementation of NaCl or by administering adrenal
cortical hormones (steroids).

claims.claim_text: Potassium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Sir Humphry Davy, Wallach records, who pried the highly reactive metal from its compounds using electrolysis — passing an electric current through them. He adds context that makes the element feel less abstract: the human body holds roughly 140 grams of potassium, and because a small fraction is the naturally radioactive isotope potassium-40, each of us carries a lifelong trace of internal background radiation.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium was first isolated by Sir Humphrey Davy
in 1807 using electrolysis as a means of separating elemental
potassium from its compounds.

claims.claim_text: Iodine is a violet-black solid element, the heaviest and one of the most reactive members of the halogen family, found in seaweed, brine wells, and the sea. In Wallach's framework it is an essential nutrient for all vertebrates: the body combines it with the amino acid (protein building block) tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the main thyroid hormone that regulates metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature. When iodine runs short -- which Wallach says is common, especially since many Americans cut back on salt on their doctors' advice -- the thyroid gland enlarges into a goiter and the body slows into hypothyroidism.
claims.verbatim:
Iodine is a violet-black solid that vaporizes to give a
violet gas. It is found in sea weed and brine wells, in the sea,
in the form of inorganic salts and organic iodides. It is the
heaviest element in the halogen family and is highly reactive.

claims.claim_text: Trace minerals differ widely in how well the gut absorbs them, and iodine is among the best. Wallach states that the metallic form of iodine is absorbed at a ratio of almost 1:1, compared with about 1:10 for iron and just 1:100 for chromium. He uses this to argue for taking the most efficient, absorbable form of trace-mineral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
For the metallic form of iodine the ratio of absorption
is almost 1:1; for iron its 1:10 and for chromium its 1:100.

claims.claim_text: Iodine takes its name from the Greek word iodes, meaning "violet-colored," a reference to the striking violet gas it gives off. It was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, who noticed a purple vapor rising from a sample of kelp to which he had added sulfuric acid. A drop of iodine will also turn starch, as in potato or flour, a deep blue.
claims.verbatim:
The color of the gas
determined its name, translated from the Greek word iodes,
meaning “violet-colored.” A drop of iodine will turn starch a
deep blue (potato, flour, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that vitamin E deficiency can directly harm reproduction. Its effects include miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy and birth defects. Deficiency can also produce muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, degeneration of the heart muscle (myocardial degeneration), softening of the brain (encephalomalacia) and liver necrosis. This reproductive link echoes vitamin E's discovery, which came from reversing infertility in rats.
claims.verbatim:
Additional symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include
miscarriage, fetal reabsorption, testicular atrophy, birth
defects, muscular dystrophy, hemolytic anemia, myocardial
degeneration, encephalomalacia and liver necrosis.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant that shields the lipids in cell membranes from peroxidation, a form of free-radical damage. Wallach explains that this ability to protect membrane fats from oxidation is directly related to vitamin E's anti-aging properties. In the same role it prevents oxidation damage to polyunsaturated fatty acids and protects cellular and mitochondrial membranes, helping keep cells from breaking down over time.
claims.verbatim:
The ability of vitamin E to protect membrane lipids from
peroxidation has been related to its anti-aging properties.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes a clearly demonstrated relationship between vitamin E, selenium, glutathione peroxidase, the amino acid cystine and the polyunsaturated fats in the cell membrane. Selenium activates glutathione peroxidase, which destroys peroxides after they form but before they can cause cell membrane damage. Vitamin E and selenium therefore act as partners in protecting cells from oxidative damage.
claims.verbatim:
A relationship between vitamin E, selenium,
glutathione peroxidase, cystine and polyunsaturated fats in
the cell membrane has been clearly demonstrated.

Selenium, which activates glutathione peroxidase, destroys
peroxides after they are produced but before they can cause
cell membrane damage.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin E, also called tocopherol, was first identified by Evans and Bishop in 1922. They observed that infertility in rats could be reversed when the animals were fed a substance isolated from vegetable oils. The vitamin was later chemically identified in 1938. Its origin in fertility research is reflected in its very name.
claims.verbatim:
Tocopherol or vitamin E was first identified by Evans
and Bishop in 1922, when they observed infertility in rats
could be reversed when they were fed a substance isolated
from vegetable oils.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin E was chemically identified in 1938 and given the name tocopherol. The word is built from the Greek 'tokos,' which translates to 'offspring.' The name reflects vitamin E's early association with fertility and successful reproduction. This ties back to its discovery through experiments on infertility in rats.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin E was chemically identified in
1938 and named tocopherol after tokos from the Greek which
translates to “offspring.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach highlights osteocalcin, a vitamin K-dependent protein now known to modulate the deposition of calcium into the bone matrix. Because of this role, he states that vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone maintenance as vitamin D. In other words, calcium needs vitamin K — not just vitamin D — to be laid down properly in bone.
claims.verbatim:
The vitamin K-dependent Gla-containing protein called
“osteocalcin” is now known to modulate calcium deposition
into bone matrix - vitamin K is as essential to healthy bone
maintenance as vitamin D.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, the coumarin anticoagulant drugs warfarin and dicumarol prevent the blood from coagulating specifically by antagonizing the action of vitamin K. Since vitamin K is required to make the clotting proteins, blocking it thins the blood. This is why these drugs and vitamin K work in direct opposition to each other.
claims.verbatim:
The coumarin anticoagulant drugs (warfarin and
dicumarol) act to prevent coagulation by antagonizing the
action of vitamin K.

claims.claim_text: Wallach considers vitamin K deficiency uncommon. It tends to occur only when the diet is low in green leafy vegetables, when the growth of intestinal flora has been inhibited by antibiotics, or when there is a fat-absorption problem. Because gut bacteria make much of our vitamin K and the vitamin is fat-soluble, both antibiotics and poor fat absorption can quietly cause a shortage.
claims.verbatim:
The deficiency of vitamin K is uncommon except when
an individuals diet is low in green leafy vegetables

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic (bleeding) disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that contained all of the then-known essential nutrients. When hog liver fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet, normal clotting time was restored. This revealed a previously unrecognized fat-soluble nutrient — vitamin K — that blood needs in order to clot.
claims.verbatim:
In 1935, Dam in Copenhagen observed a fatal hemorrhagic
disease in newly hatched chickens fed a laboratory diet that
contained all of the known essential nutrients. When hog liver
fat extract or alfalfa was added to the diet normal clotting time
was restored.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework a biotin deficiency in humans produces a progressive loss of both hair and hair color. Alongside the hair changes he describes skin lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia and paresthesia (especially in the extremities), muscle pain, conjunctivitis, and blepharitis.
claims.verbatim:
Symptoms of biotin deficiency in humans include skin
lesions over the nose and mouth, depression, hyperesthesia
and _ paresthesia particularly over the extremities, muscle
pain, conjunctivitis, blepharitis and a progressive loss of hair

and hair color.

claims.claim_text: Biotin, also known as vitamin H or coenzyme R, was first isolated in 1936 and synthesized in 1943. Its deficiency was originally observed in chicks and rats fed raw egg whites, which were later found to contain an egg-white-injury factor.
claims.verbatim:
Biotin or vitamin H (coenzyme R) was first isolated in
1936 and synthesized in 1943.

claims.claim_text: Choline is an essential nutrient with a vitamin-like coenzyme function that Wallach groups among the water-soluble vitamins. It has been recognized as essential for more than a hundred years. Choline serves as a structural building block of all cell membranes, plasma lipoproteins and lung surfactant, and in the nervous system it forms sphingomyelin and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. It also carries fat out of the liver, so a shortage leads to a fatty liver. The body can make some choline from the amino acids methionine or serine with vitamin B12 and folate, but not enough to meet daily needs, which is why it must be supplied through diet or supplements.
claims.verbatim:
Choline has been known for more than 100 years as
being essential and it has a vitamin-like coenzyme function.

claims.claim_text: Choline is an essential nutrient that has been known to be essential for more than a hundred years, and it acts with a vitamin-like coenzyme function. Wallach counts it among the nutrients the body must obtain because, although the body can make some of it internally, it cannot make enough to meet daily needs.
claims.verbatim:
Choline has been known for more than 100 years as
being essential and it has a vitamin-like coenzyme function.

claims.claim_text: Wallach classifies choline as a water-soluble vitamin, placing it in the same group as the B-complex vitamins, biotin and vitamin C. He describes water-soluble vitamins as essential nutrients that function in the metabolic processes of all living cells.
claims.verbatim:
2) Water soluble - B-complex, biotin, choline and
vitamin C - Water soluble vitamins consists of 10 separate
water soluble B vitamins and vitamin C.

claims.claim_text: Choline is a component of the phospholipid sphingomyelin, an important part of the brain and peripheral nerves. Because it is a precursor for the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, choline is directly involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.
claims.verbatim:
Choline is also a component of another phospholipid,
sphingomyelin, which is an important component of the
brain and peripheral nerves. As a precursor for acetylcholine,
choline is involved in the transmission of nerve impulses.

claims.claim_text: Choline is part of fat metabolism and the transport of fat out of the liver, so a deficiency can result in a fatty liver. Working through phospholipids, it carries triglycerides and forms lecithin in the liver, a process that removes fatty acids from the liver's glycerides and lowers the triglyceride level. Wallach warns that in a severe form, choline-deficient fatty liver can land a person on a liver transplant list.
claims.verbatim:
The function of choline in humans is part of the
metabolism of and in the transport of fat from the liver. A
deficiency of choline can result ina fatty liver. Asa component
of phospholipids, choline functions in triglyceride transport
and in cell membrane structure. In the liver, choline forms
lecithin (phosphatidyl choline). During this process, fatty
acids are removed from the glycerides of the liver, thus
reducing the triglyceride level.

claims.claim_text: The body can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine or serine, a process that requires vitamin B12 and folacin (folate). However, the rate of that internal synthesis is too slow to meet daily requirements, which is exactly why Wallach counts choline as an essential nutrient that must be supplied.
claims.verbatim:
Man can synthesize choline from the amino acids methionine
or serine in the presence of vitamin B12 and folacin. The rate at
which choline can be synthesized is insufficient to meet daily
requirements and for this reason it is considered an essential
nutrient.

claims.claim_text: Because choline is a raw material for acetylcholine — a key nerve-signaling chemical — and a building block of the brain's and nerves' insulating sphingomyelin, Wallach reports it has real value in movement disorders.
