claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, when samarium was discovered in 1879 its spectral absorption lines were first identified in a mineral called samarskite. He notes that samarskite itself was named for a Russian army officer, Colonel Samarski, tying the mineral in which the element was found back to that officer.
claims.verbatim:
spectral absorption lines in a mineral called
samarskite, which has been named for a Russian army officer,
Colonel Samarski.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, ytterbium was discovered in 1878 by the French chemist Jean de Marignac, who found it within the mineral erbia -- which, in his telling, made it the first 'rare earth' element ever discovered. Its name comes from Ytterby, a small Swedish village. Wallach adds that the main source of ytterbium is monazite sand -- a material that holds all of the rare earths along with thorium and calcium -- recovered from river sand in India and Brazil and from beach sand in Florida.
claims.verbatim:
The French chemist Jean de Marignac discovered this
element in 1878 as a part of the mineral known as erbia and
was the first “rare earth” element discovered. It was named for
the Swedish village of Ytterby. The main source of ytterbium
is monazite sand which contains all of the rare earths, thorium
and calcium and is found in river sand from India and Brazil
and beach sand from Florida at three hundredths of one per
cent.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that holmium was first detected in 1878, when two Swiss chemists noticed its characteristic spectral lines but could not identify the element responsible, so they referred to it only as "element X." A year later, in 1879, the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified it and gave it the name Holmia, after his home town of Stockholm. In Wallach's survey holmium is one of the rare-earth trace minerals, scattered thinly through rocks, plants and animals and collecting mainly in bone in land animals.
claims.verbatim:
In 1878, two Swiss chemists noticed holmium’s
characteristic spectral lines, but could not identify them, so
they referred to the unknown element as “element X.” In 1879,
a Swedish chemist, Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified
the element and called it Holmia, Latin for his home town of
Stockholm.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, holmium takes its name from Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm, the home town of the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, who isolated and identified the element in 1879. The element had first been noticed a year earlier, in 1878, through its distinctive spectral lines, before Cleve pinned it down and named it. So the name of this rare-earth trace mineral is essentially a Latin tribute to Cleve's own home town.
claims.verbatim:
In 1879,
a Swedish chemist, Per Teodor Cleve isolated and identified
the element and called it Holmia, Latin for his home town of
Stockholm.

claims.claim_text: In Immortality, Wallach traces tantalum's name to Greek mythology. Its discoverer, the Swedish chemist Anders Gustav Ekeberg, found the new element in 1802 near the Swedish town of Ytterby, and named it for Tantalos, the father of Niobe. Wallach notes that Ytterby played an important role in the history of chemistry, serving as a source of minerals for the discovery of the rare earths. So the element carries a mythological namesake tied to one of science's most important mineral-discovery locales.
claims.verbatim:
Anders Gustav Ekeberg, aSwedish chemist, discovered
the new element in 1802 near the Swedish town of Ytterby,
which played an important role in the history of chemistry,
particularly as a source of minerals for the discovery of rare
earths.

Ekeberg named his new element for Tantalos, the father

claims.claim_text: Wallach relates that tantalum had a rocky start as a recognized element. For almost 50 years after Ekeberg announced his discovery, many chemists believed he had actually confused tantalum with niobium. The matter was not settled until pure tantalum metal was finally produced in 1903 -- more than a century after the 1802 discovery. Wallach frames the mix-up within the element's mythological pedigree, noting it was named for Tantalos, the father of Niobe, queen of the city of Thebes.
claims.verbatim:
of Niobe, who, in Greek mythology, was queen of the city of
Thebes. For almost 50 years after Ekeberg’s announcement
of his new element, many chemist thought he had confused
tantalum with niobium. Pure tantalum metal was not
produced until 1903.

claims.claim_text: In his survey of tantalum, Wallach reports that the element is used for dental and joint prosthesis. Its principal ore is the mineral columbite, which he says is widely distributed throughout the world, with large deposits in Africa, Thailand, Portugal and Canada. These are among the few concrete real-world uses and sources Wallach records for this rare, plant-derived trace mineral.
claims.verbatim:
The principal ore of tantalum is the mineral columbite,
which is widely distributed throughout the world, with large
deposits in Africa, Thailand, Portugal and Canada. Tantalum
is used for dental and joint prosthesis.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's account, hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal whose elemental properties and history are inseparable from those of its 'twin,' the element zirconium. Hafnium is actually more dense than zirconium, yet the two metals are so chemically similar that it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other. Wallach also lists hafnium among his 60 essential elements and among the plant-derived minerals of a high-quality humic shale, trace minerals that, though not 'classically' considered essential, he holds meet the criteria of an essential nutrient.
claims.verbatim:
Hafnium is a bright, silvery-white metal, its elemental
properties and history are joined with the element zirconium.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that hafnium was finally found by Dirk Coster, a Dutch physicist, and George Karl von Hevesy, a Hungarian physicist. To honor Bohr, the two named their new element after his native city, Copenhagen, using the Latin translation of that city's name, Hafnia. So the metal's name is a tribute both to the city of Copenhagen and to Bohr himself.
claims.verbatim:
Ultimately, Dirk Coster, a Dutch
physicist and George Karl von Hevesy, a Hungarian physicist
found the element. To honor Bohr, Coster and de Hevesy
named their new element for his native city, Copenhagen,
using the Latin translation, Hafnia.

claims.claim_text: Zirconium is a mineral Wallach counts among the essential trace elements and rare earths, and its best-known and most familiar form is the mineral zircon -- a crystalline compound of zirconium silicate. Zircon occurs in a wide variety of colors, and once cut and polished it is prized as a semiprecious gem. Because it has a very high index of refraction, bending light through large angles, colorless zircon crystals are so brilliant that they are often used as a diamond substitute in imitation jewelry.
claims.verbatim:
Zircon is a crystalline compound of zirconium silicate
(ZrSiO,). Itis found ina variety of colors, and when the crystal
is cut and polished, the stone is regarded as a semiprecious
gem. Zircon has a very high index of refraction, which means
that it has the property of bending light through large angles.
Because the colorless crystals of zircon have a high brilliance
they are oftentimes used as a diamond substitute in faux

jewelry.

claims.claim_text: Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. Its best-known compound, the mineral zircon, is far older as a known substance -- it has been recognized since ancient times and is even referred to in the Bible. So while the element itself was a comparatively late chemical discovery, the stone that carries it had been prized long before.
claims.verbatim:
Zirconium was discovered in 1787 by the German
chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth. The best known compound
of zirconium is the mineral zircon. This mineral has been
known since ancient times and is even referred to in the Bible.

claims.claim_text: Zirconium takes its name from the mineral zircon, and 'zircon' in turn comes from 'zargun,' the Arabic name for the stone. 'Zargun' translates to 'gold color.' So the element's name traces back through Arabic to a word describing the color of the crystal it was first known in.
claims.verbatim:
Zirconium derives its name from zargun, which is the Arabic
name for zircon and translates to “gold color.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes zirconium and hafnium as closely bound twin metals. Although hafnium is more dense than zirconium, the two are chemically so similar that it is almost impossible to work with one without working with the other. Their elemental properties and history are intertwined -- zirconium's ever-present, diamond-like presence long overshadowed hafnium, which is one reason hafnium was not discovered until 1923 even though it is a common, abundant metal.
claims.verbatim:
Hafnium, is more dense than zirconium, however, the two
metals are chemically similar and it is almost impossible to
work with one without working with the other.

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to controlled feeding studies as his hard evidence for the rare earths. When rare-earth minerals were added to laboratory animals' diets — on top of the recognized major and trace minerals — the animals' expected lifespan doubled across several different species. He holds these same rare earths are vital to animal (and most probably human) health and longevity, yet they have been stripped from our modern food supply, so in his framework daily supplementation is the only reliable way to get enough.
claims.verbatim:
Rare Earths added to laboratory animal's diets as a
supplement to the well recognized major and trace minerals
have doubled the expected life span of several different
species.

claims.claim_text: Nitrates are salt compounds formed when nitric acid is neutralized by bases such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. Wallach explains they are added to canned foods and cured, preserved meats to prevent bacteria from growing and to keep the meat colored red. His health concern is what happens after you eat them: in the acid environment of the stomach, nitrates (and the related nitrites) are converted into nitrosamines, compounds that can become cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) and can suppress thyroid function. For that reason he classes both dietary nitrates (deli slices, sandwich meats) and water-borne nitrates among the "goitrogens" — substances that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism and can produce thyroid disease.
claims.verbatim:
When nitric acid is neutralized with bases including
sodium and potassium hydroxide, it forms compounds called
nitrates. Nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and
preserved meats to help prevent the growth of bacteria and to
color meat red.

Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

claims.claim_text: Nitrites are preservative compounds added, alongside nitrates, to canned foods and cured or preserved meats — bacon, ham, sausage, bologna, salami, pepperoni, jerky and deli meats — to stop bacteria from growing and to keep the meat looking red. Wallach's warning is about what happens once they are eaten: in the acid environment of the stomach, nitrites (and nitrates) are converted into nitrosamines, compounds that can turn into cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) and can suppress thyroid function. He therefore counts nitrites among the "goitrogens" that interfere with normal thyroid metabolism, and lists them among the dietary free radicals a person should cut down on to slow aging.
claims.verbatim:
Nitrates and nitrites are added to canned foods and
preserved meats to help prevent the growth of bacteria and to
color meat red.

Nitrates and nitrites are converted to nitrosamines in
the acid environment of the stomach; these compounds can
be converted to cancer causing chemicals (carcinogens) and
can suppress thyroid function.

claims.claim_text: Berylliosis is a painful and sometimes fatal lung disease caused by inhaling beryllium oxide dust, which is released as a contaminant during the mining and industrial handling of the metal. Beryllium itself is a mineral — the scientific name of the gemstone beryl is beryllium aluminum silicate — so the hazard comes not from the element in food but from breathing its powdered oxide. Wallach describes two forms: an acute form (acute beryllium disease, or chemical pneumonitis) first reported in Europe in 1933 and in the United States in 1943, and a chronic form — chronic berylliosis — that resembles pulmonary sarcoidosis, another chronic lung disease.
claims.verbatim:
Inhalation of beryllium oxide dust (mining and
industrial contaminants) can lead to “berylliosis,” a painful
and sometimes fatal lung disease.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes the rare earths as a whole category of chemically very similar metal oxides, not a single element. He says they are drawn from minerals that are widely distributed across the earth yet relatively scarce, and treats this large family of related metals as one class.
claims.verbatim:
The term, rare earths, refers to any of a large series of
very similar oxides of metals obtained from widely distributed
but relatively scarce minerals.

claims.claim_text: According to Wallach, reaching first for high-fructose-corn-syrup-laden soft drinks is a sign of mineral deficiency rather than simple thirst. Chromium and vanadium deficiencies manifest as an intense thirst for liquid — and minerally deficient people reach for HFCS soft drinks first and plain water last — together with a hunger for carbohydrates such as soft drinks, sweetened coffee and tea, alcohol, pasta, desserts, and bread.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested
by an intense thirst for liquid (high fructose corn syrup laden
soft drinks being the usual first choice and water the last for
minerally deficient humans) and hunger for carbohydrates
(i.e. - soft drinks, coffee and tea with added sugar, alcohol,
pasta, deserts, bread, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that high-fructose corn syrup is a manufactured sweetener made from grains (corn) as well as from sugar beet and sugar cane. Fructose — also called levulose or fruit sugar — occurs naturally with glucose and sucrose in honey and fruit and is the sweetest of the natural sugars; sweeteners containing glucose and levulose are processed from these crops to make high-fructose corn syrup.
claims.verbatim:
Fructose: (levulose, fruit sugar) is found together with
glucose and sucrose in honey and fruit. It is the sweetest of the
natural sugars. Sweeteners containing glucose and levulose
can be made from grains (corn) as well as from the sugar beet
and sugar cane to make high-fructose corn syrup.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in the 1940s professors A.H. Carlson and F. Holzol added a "creative twist" to the caloric-restriction (CR) longevity approach by testing intermittent periods of fasting in rats. The animals were free-choice fed a high-quality diet rich in vitamins and minerals in unlimited amounts, but were fasted completely every other day (one group), every third day (another group), or every fourth day (a third group). As Wallach reports the result, the un-fasted rats reached a maximum life span of 800 days, while all three intermittently fasted groups extended maximum life span to 1,000 to 1,100 days — a 20 to 30% increase. Wallach presents intermittent fasting here as a variant of his "under-nutrition without malnutrition" theme: the fasting is paired with a nutrient-dense diet on the eating days, not with starvation.
claims.verbatim:
In the 1940s, professors A.H. Carlson and F. Holzol
added a creative twist to the concept of the CR diet by studying
the effects of intermittent periods of fasting on the life span
of rats. They free choice fed rats a high-quality diet rich in
vitamins and minerals in unlimited amounts, but fasted them
completely every other day; another group was fasted every
third day and another group fasted every fourth day.

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites Dr. Charles Goodrick of the National Institute on Aging (Gerontology Research Unit), who studied intermittent fasting by giving the control group a "perfect diet" while fasting the study group every other day. According to Wallach, the every-other-day fasted rats increased maximum life span from 875 days (the normally fed rats) to 1,295 days, and raised the 50% survival point from 630 days to 980 days. Wallach presents this as further evidence that intermittent fasting — alternating fed days with complete fast days on a nutrient-rich diet — increases both the average and the maximum life span of animals.
claims.verbatim:
Dr. Charles Goodrick of the National Institute on
